name: Hezekiah
bio:
Hezekiah succeeded his father Ahaz as king of Judah after Ahaz was buried with his ancestors in the City of David (2 Kings 16:20).

## 📖 Core Story: Reform, Rebellion, and Sennacherib's Siege

Hezekiah began to reign at twenty-five, in Hoshea's third year as king of Israel, and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem; his mother was Abi, daughter of Zachariah. He did right in the LORD's eyes like David, removing the high places, smashing sacred stones, cutting down the Asherah poles, and even breaking up the bronze serpent Moses had made, since Israel had taken to worshipping it. Scripture says none of Judah's kings before or after him trusted the LORD so completely.

Chronicles opens his reign with an extensive account of this reform. In the very first month of his first year, Hezekiah reopened and repaired the temple doors his father had shut, gathered the priests and Levites, and charged them to consecrate themselves and clear out the filth his father's generation had left behind, explaining that Judah's recent calamities were punishment for abandoning the LORD's house. The Levites sanctified the temple over sixteen days, carrying its uncleanness out to the Kidron Valley and restoring the vessels Ahaz had discarded. Hezekiah and the city's officials then offered a sin offering for the whole kingdom, and amid trumpets and the songs of David, Asaph, and Gad and Nathan's instruments, the people worshiped as the first burnt offering in years went up on the altar. The congregation then brought so many sacrifices and thank offerings that the priests, too few for the work, needed the Levites' help to keep pace — the Levites, Chronicles notes, were more conscientious about consecrating themselves than the priests were. Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced that God had moved them to do all this so suddenly (2 Chronicles 29:1-36).

With the priests not yet fully consecrated and the people not yet assembled in time for Passover's normal date, Hezekiah and the leaders decided to keep it a month late instead, and sent letters throughout Israel and Judah — even to the northern tribes Assyria had not yet fully scattered — urging them to return to the LORD and come celebrate in Jerusalem. Most of the messengers were mocked and ridiculed, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came, while in Judah God gave the people one heart to obey. The assembled crowd tore down Jerusalem's pagan altars and kept the Passover, though so many had not properly purified themselves that the Levites had to slaughter the lambs on their behalf; Hezekiah prayed that the LORD would pardon everyone who sincerely sought him despite this uncleanness, and the LORD healed the people. The joyful festival, extended a further seven days by popular demand and funded generously by Hezekiah and the officials, became the greatest celebration in Jerusalem since Solomon's time (2 Chronicles 30:1-27).

He rebelled against Assyria, refusing to serve its king, and struck the Philistines as far as Gaza (2 Kings 18:1-8).

In his sixth year, Shalmaneser of Assyria finally captured Samaria and deported Israel, a judgment for Israel's covenant-breaking (2 Kings 18:9-12). In his fourteenth year, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, captured all of Judah's fortified cities; Hezekiah tried to buy him off, emptying the temple and palace treasuries and even stripping gold from the temple doors, but Sennacherib still sent his officers Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great army against Jerusalem. Hezekiah's officials Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah went out to meet them, and Rabshakeh delivered a mocking speech, questioning Hezekiah's trust in both Egypt and the LORD, and shouting directly to the people on the wall in Hebrew that no nation's god had ever saved them from Assyria. The people, under royal order, said nothing in reply, and Hezekiah's officials returned to him with their clothes torn (2 Kings 18:13-37).

## 📖 Core Story: Prayer, and the Angel's Deliverance

Hearing Rabshakeh's report, Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went to the temple, sending his officials to ask the prophet Isaiah to pray for the besieged remnant. Isaiah assured them Sennacherib would withdraw and fall by the sword in his own land. When Sennacherib sent a second, more detailed threatening letter, Hezekiah spread it before the LORD in the temple and prayed that the LORD would save Jerusalem so all the earth would know he alone was God. Isaiah then delivered a detailed oracle: the LORD had heard Hezekiah's prayer, mocked Sennacherib's arrogance, and promised Jerusalem would not fall — Sennacherib would return the way he came, not even shooting an arrow into the city. That night the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp; by morning Sennacherib had withdrawn to Nineveh, where he was later assassinated by his own sons (2 Kings 19:1-37).

## 📖 Core Story: Illness, Healing, and a Fateful Pride

Hezekiah fell sick to the point of death, and Isaiah told him to put his affairs in order, for he would not recover. Hezekiah wept and prayed, reminding the LORD of his faithful service, and before Isaiah had even left the palace, the LORD sent him back with a different message: Hezekiah's prayer was heard, and fifteen years would be added to his life. As a sign, Isaiah had the shadow on Ahaz's sundial move backward ten steps instead of forward, confirming the LORD's word (2 Kings 20:1-11).

When Berodach-Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with a gift after hearing of Hezekiah's illness, Hezekiah proudly showed them everything in his treasuries and armory. Isaiah rebuked him for it, prophesying that everything shown to them, and more, would one day be carried off to Babylon, and Hezekiah's own descendants would become eunuchs in the Babylonian palace. Hezekiah responded only that the word of the LORD was good, since peace would last in his own days. Hezekiah also built a pool and tunnel to bring water into Jerusalem. He died and was succeeded by his son Manasseh (2 Kings 20:12-21).
